name: Resistance bands

lead: Resistance bands are elastic loops or tubes, usually latex or fabric-covered rubber, that provide tension that rises as they are stretched. They are sold in graded strengths and weigh almost nothing, so they travel and store easily.

In appearance-oriented training they are used in two ways: as a low-cost way to build muscle in the shoulders, arms, back and glutes at home, and as the standard tool for posture work such as face pulls, band pull-aparts and external rotations that strengthen the upper back and rotator cuff muscles that counter a rounded-shoulder look.

paras: Muscle responds to mechanical tension and effort rather than to the specific type of resistance. Bands load the muscle most at the lengthened or end range of a movement, and trained to near failure they produce strength gains comparable to conventional equipment in the trials pooled so far. Progression comes from thicker bands, doubling up, shortening the anchor distance or slowing the tempo.

Bands can snap or slip if they are nicked, over-stretched or anchored badly, and a recoil to the face or eye is the recognized injury. Latex allergy is a consideration. Resistance is hard to quantify, which makes tracking progressive overload less precise than with plates, and bands top out for heavy lower-body work. The claim that bands can build real muscle is supported; the idea that they are superior to weights is not.
